title: Echoing and answering the trumpet
summary: Ridgley says players answered each other, and that everything was practiced until it harmonized.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Rigley, did you ever, when you were playing your trombone parts, try to echo the trumpet part or any other part?
No. Now what you mean by echo?
Answering. Oh yes, you had that to do. A better time, yeah.
Was that a good thing to do?

I mean. It was all right, yeah. We got a lot of fire in him and things like that. We got it down, we got his pep, you know, and what he was going to do. How he'd play it, I'd answer him while I'd do it, he'd answer me. That'd go, you see.
Would you answer him exactly, or would you?

In your court. In your court, yeah. You had to have the right court, you see, whatever it was. But both of his would harmonize together. I see. See, you couldn't make no mess of it. Sometimes some fella would be hitting an A, another fella would be hitting something else that wouldn't sound good. But you'd practice those things together. We practiced everything we played. It didn't come out of nothing. If it didn't sound good, we wouldn't play it until we did get it down. And we wanted to come out and make a hit.
